result.answer:
Verdict: SUPPORTED

**Evidence for:** The relevant paper reports a case-control study of 6,110 elderly New Jersey residents [S:f4a354ac59ac#3]. Use of statins in the prior 180 days (adjusted OR, 0.50; 95% CI, 0.33-0.76) and prior 3 years (adjusted OR, 0.57; 95% CI, 0.40-0.82) was associated with a significant reduction in hip fracture risk [S:f4a354ac59ac#4]. Current statin use was associated with a 71% reduction in risk (adjusted OR, 0.29; 95% CI, 0.10-0.81) [S:f4a354ac59ac#5]. The authors conclude that these findings support an association between statin use by elderly patients and reduction in the risk of hip fracture [S:f4a354ac59ac#9].

**Evidence against:** The paper cautions that controlled trials are needed to exclude the possibility of unmeasured confounders [S:f4a354ac59ac#9].

citations.title: scifact-1290 - 4687948.md
citations.text:
[0] CONTEXT Recent animal studies have found that 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A
(HMG-CoA) lipid-lowering drugs (statins) substantially increase bone formation, but whether statin use in
humans results in clinically meaningful bone formation or a reduction in the risk of osteoporotic fractures
is not known.
[1] OBJECTIVE To determine whether the use of statins is associated with reduced hip fracture risk.
[2] DESIGN Case-control study.
[3] SETTING AND PATIENTS A total of 6110 New Jersey residents aged 65 years or older and enrolled
in Medicare and either Medicaid or the Pharmacy Assistance for the Aged and Disabled program.
[4] Case patients (n=1222) underwent surgical repair of a hip fracture in 1994.
[5] Control patients (n=4888) were identified at a ratio of 4:1 and frequency-matched to case patients for
age and sex.

citations.title: scifact-1290 - 4687948.md
citations.text:
[6] MAIN OUTCOME MEASURE Adjusted odds ratio (OR) of hip fracture by statin use in the 180 days
and 3 years prior to the index date (the earliest date of admission for surgery), adjusted for demographic
and clinical characteristics and health care utilization.
[7] RESULTS Use of statins in either the prior 180 days (adjusted OR, 0.50; 95% confidence interval [CI],
0.33-0.76) or prior 3 years (adjusted OR, 0.57; 95% CI, 0.40-0.82) was associated with a significant
reduction in the risk of hip fracture, even after controlling for variables such as race, insurance status,
psychoactive medications, estrogen and thiazide use, ischemic heart disease, cancer, and diabetes
mellitus.
[8] No significant relationship was observed between use of nonstatin lipid-lowering agents and hip
fracture risk.

citations.title: scifact-1290 - 4687948.md
citations.text:
[9] Clear relationships were observed between the degree of reduction in hip fracture risk and the extent
of statin use; there was no evidence of such relationships with nonstatin lipid-lowering agents.
[10] After adjusting for extent of statin use in the prior 3 years, current use (on the index date) was
associated with a 71% reduction in risk (adjusted OR, 0.29; 95% CI, 0.10-0.81).

citations.title: scifact-1290 - 4687948.md
citations.text:
[12] Use of nonstatin lipid-lowering agents was not observed to be associated with reduction in hip
fracture risk in any of these alternative models or analyses.
[13] CONCLUSIONS These findings support an association between statin use by elderly patients and
reduction in the risk of hip fracture.
[14] Controlled trials are needed to exclude the possibility of unmeasured confounders.
[15] JAMA.
[16] 2000;283:3211-3216
